The Joint Action Committee of the University of Abuja has called on President Bola Tinubu to intervene in the controversy surrounding the university’s land, demanding the reversal of all allocations made by the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike. The committee, comprising the university’s staff unions, student leaders and representatives of the National Association of Nigerian Students, said the institution’s 11,824.04 hectares of land must be protected from what it described as unauthorised allocations. In a statement released on Tuesday, the unions also demanded that the Federal Government honour its December 2025 agreement with the Academic Staff Union of Universities to proactively protect university land and landed properties. The statement was signed by the ASUU Chairman, Professor Sylvanus Ugoh; JAC and SSANU Chairman, Nurudeen Yusuf; NASU Chairman, Sadiya Ibrahim Hassan; NAAT Chairman, Ugochukwu Agumuo; and SUG President, Peculiar Eyamu. The JAC faulted a report allegedly recommending the reduction of the university’s main campus land from 11,824.04 hectares to 4,519.80 hectares, insisting that the institution was neither involved in its preparation nor approved its recommendations. It said the main committee established by the FCT Minister in December 2020 to address encroachment, resettlement of indigenous communities, removal of illegal structures and provision of infrastructure held only its inaugural meeting in April 2021. The unions alleged that the university’s representatives were presented with a report by a separate technical committee at a meeting at the Federal Capital Development Authority on March 15, 2022, but rejected it because they were not involved in its deliberations. The JAC challenged the FCTA to produce a copy of the report bearing the signatures of the university’s representatives rather than merely presenting a list of committee members. Defending the institution’s landholding, the unions said about 30 per cent of the 11,824.04 hectares was undevelopable because of the Kuku Hills, the National Rail Corridor buffer zones and 330KV high-voltage power lines. They also dismissed allegations that the university was selling portions of its land, describing the claim as “totally false and misleading”. According to the committee, Section 22 of the University of Abuja Act regulates the use of the institution’s land and does not provide for its sale. It explained that the siting of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission Academy on the campus was a partnership arrangement in line with the university’s community service mandate. The unions further argued that the university’s 38 years of existence did not mean it had failed to develop its land, noting that institutional development was usually undertaken in phases and depended largely on government funding. “Unions are the protectors and defenders of our institutions and that is why we will resist the impunity of the Hon Minister regarding University of Abuja land with all our might,” the statement added. The JAC demanded the reversal of all land allocations made by Wike on the university’s property, implementation of the December 2025 agreement with ASUU and urgent intervention by Tinubu, who is also the university’s Visitor. The controversy followed Monday’s protest by workers, students and other stakeholders over the disputed land allocations. The FCTA had defended Wike’s decision, saying it was based on recommendations by a committee established in 2016 under a former FCT Minister, Mohammed Musa Bello. The minister’s spokesman, Lere Olayinka, said the committee recommended reducing the university’s land allocation, adding that Wike approved 4,519.80 hectares instead of the 100 hectares reportedly recommended. The dispute has also been taken to court, with the university challenging the disputed land decisions.
